title: Clever Hans the counting horse was really reading his questioners’ faces

cover.alt: The horse Clever Hans standing in front of a board of numbers and pointing at one with his nose, in an early 1900s photograph.

body: Around 1904, a horse in Germany named Hans seemed to add, subtract, tell the time and spell, tapping out answers with a hoof. A 13-person commission led by the psychologist Carl Stumpf found no trick. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst tested Hans properly: the horse answered correctly nearly nine times out of ten when he could see a questioner who knew the answer, but almost never when he could not see them. Hans was reading tiny changes in posture and expression that told him when to stop tapping, cues his questioners did not know they were giving.

slides.question: What share of answers did Hans get right when he could not see the questioner?
slides.explanation: About 6%: 2 correct answers in 35 trials. With a visible questioner who knew the answer, he scored 89% (50 of 56).

slides.heading: A lesson for science
slides.text: The Clever Hans effect, named after Pfungst’s work, is one reason experiments are now double-blind: if the person running a test knows the answer, they can leak it without meaning to. The same worry applies to drug-sniffing dogs reacting to their handlers, and to AI models that learn unintended shortcuts.

slides.question: What finally exposed how Hans was doing it?
slides.explanation: Pfungst used blinders and questioners who did not know the answer. Hans failed when he could not see a person who knew it.
